name: Yerisiam
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Kamholz, David C. 2014. Austronesians in Papua: Diversification and change in South Halmahera-West New Guinea. PhD dissertation, University of California, Berkeley (eScholarship qt8zg8b1vd). Corroborated by Kamholz, David. 2017. Tone and language contact in southern Cenderawasih Bay. NUSA 62: 7-39.
catalog_locator: Kamholz 2014, ch. 5 'Tonal phonology', sec. 5.3.2 'Yerisiam', p. 106; diachronic stress remark p. 109; summary sec. 5.4 p. 117. Same text in Kamholz 2017 NUSA 62 sec. 3.2, pp. 18-21 and fn. 3 p. 9.
catalog_quote: Yerisiam has both contrastive tone and vowel length. The tone-bearing unit is the mora, with short vowels counted as a single mora, long vowels counted as two moras, and diphthongs variably counted as one or two moras (see below). Two underlying tones may be associated with moras: high (H) and low (L). It follows that contour tones may be realized only as the sequences HL and LH on long vowels and bimoraic diphthongs. [...] Three groups of common tonal patterns can be identified. Pattern 1 consists of high tone throughout the word (H). Pattern 2 consists of initial high tone followed by a shift to low on some mora (HL). Pattern 3 consists of initial low tone, with a shift to high on the final syllable (L*H). [...] [p. 109] Of the 70 words with patterns 1 and 2, 46 have a long vowel on the historically penultimate syllable. The most plausible explanation for this is that Yerisiam descends from a proto-language that had penultimate stress, with former stress surviving as vowel length. [...] [p. 117] Traces of former penultimate stress were found in Maˈya, Moor, and Yerisiam.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Yerisiam is analysed as a word-tone language (underlying H and L linked to moras; three dominant lexical melodies H, H..L, L*H, the last treated as default/toneless) with contrastive vowel length; the author gives no synchronic word-stress rule. Stress is mentioned only historically: Proto-SHWNG penultimate stress is said to survive as vowel length on the historically penultimate syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. (For the length-from-stress correlation: 24 of 70 etymologised words lack the expected long penult; kinship terms, pronouns, numeral 'four' flagged as likely contaminated.) NUSA 2017 fn 3 concedes some length/tone facts might be reanalysable as stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical word/root melodies from an 1802-item lexicon; tonal alternations with pronominal prefixes and the enclitic =tà discussed; analysis explicitly 'not a full-scale instrumental or phonological analysis' (2017: 9).
new_statements.identity_note: Sources describe Yerisiam [ire] = Glottolog ires1239 (Kamholz spells it Yerisiam; Glottolog ref title uses 'Yeresiam'; older name Iresim). Data from Kamholz's own fieldwork (2010-2013) in the Yerisiam-speaking villages west of Nabire, southern Cenderawasih Bay; no dialect split reported.

sources.note: Ch. 5 'Tonal phonology', sec. 5.3.2 Yerisiam (pp. 106-116): Yerisiam has contrastive tone (H, L; TBU = mora) and contrastive vowel length; three common word-tone patterns (H, HL, L*H; pattern 3 analysed as underlyingly toneless/default). No synchronic word-stress rule is given. Stress appears only diachronically: p. 109 'Yerisiam descends from a proto-language that had penultimate stress, with former stress surviving as vowel length'; sec. 5.4 p. 117 'Traces of former penultimate stress were found in Ma'ya, Moor, and Yerisiam.'

sources.citation: Kamholz, David. 2017. Tone and language contact in southern Cenderawasih Bay. NUSA: Linguistic studies of languages in and around Indonesia 62: 7-39.
sources.note: Sec. 3.2 Yerisiam (pp. 18-24) repeats the dissertation analysis nearly verbatim: contrastive tone (H/L on moras) plus vowel length; speakers produce tonal contrasts consistently (p. 9). Only stress remark is historical (p. 21): 'Proto-SHWNG penultimate stress straightforwardly accounts for this, with former stress surviving as vowel length.' Footnote 3 (p. 9) concedes that what is analysed as length or tone might in some cases be reanalysable as stress.

sources.citation: Kamholz, David. 2012. Yeresiam: A tonal Austronesian language of the Bird's Neck. 6 pp. handout (Glottolog hh:312203).
sources.access_detail: open copy posted by the author (located 2026-09-25); a digital copy (available on request)
sources.quote: Two tones: H and L. TBU is the mora: each vowel can have its own tone. Orthography: H = acute, L = grave; unmarked vowels have the same tone as the next marked vowel to the left, so díijanà 'fish' = dííjánà. Most common tonal patterns: H throughout: áaka 'bite'; H switching to L at some point: áakà 'four', áàka 'small sago rib'; L switching to H in the final syllable: àká 'ball sago'. However, many other tonal patterns are possible.
sources.locator: section 2.4 Tone, printed p. 2; pattern table printed p. 3
sources.note: The only Glottolog descriptive ref; a dedicated phonology handout might state explicitly whether there is any stress/prominence independent of tone and length. Likely superseded by Kamholz 2014/2017 but unverified.
